Six EE Projects That
See With Light
Lasers, photodiodes, and time-of-flight — six builds that measure, map, and
talk using light. From a beam-break speed trap to a spinning LiDAR that draws
your room as a point cloud, to sending audio across the room on a laser. Cheap
optics; real photonics signal processing.

❯ project 01
Optical Break-Beam Speed Trap
Fire a laser across a gap and clock anything that crosses it — in real units

$15
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters

The simplest thing you can do with light is notice when it stops arriving. Point a laser at a
photodiode and you have a beam; break it and a voltage collapses in microseconds. Put two
beams a known distance apart, time how long an object takes to cross from one to the other,
and you have a speed trap — clock a Nerf dart, a dropped ball, a swinging door. It is the
cheapest possible photonics build, the response is instant and visual, and it teaches the
photodetection front end that every later project in this guide depends on.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand photodiode and phototransistor detection, turning a light level into a
clean logic edge with a comparator, microsecond-scale timing on a microcontroller, and
converting a time interval into a physical measurement — the core of optical sensing and
instrumentation.

→ the job this maps to: optical sensing & instrumentation — industrial automation, robotics,
and test-and-measurement teams.

! LASER EYE SAFETY
Lasers can damage eyes. Use only low-power Class 1 / 2 modules (a few mW), never look
into the beam or aim it at anyone, and remember infrared lasers are invisible — you
cannot tell they are on. Set beams below eye level and keep this in mind for every build
in this guide.

Light to current: A photodiode (or phototransistor) turns incident light into a small
current. A laser aimed at it holds that current high; break the beam and it collapses. A
load resistor turns the current into a voltage you can read.

Clean edge with a comparator: The raw photodiode voltage is analog and noisy. A comparator
(or Schmitt trigger) with a threshold turns “beam present / broken” into a crisp digital
edge — immune to ambient drift — that a microcontroller can timestamp.

Two beams, one interval: Place two beams a measured distance d apart along the path. The
object breaks beam A, then beam B; the microcontroller measures Δt between the two edges.
Speed = d / Δt.

Microsecond timing: For a fast projectile, Δt is sub-millisecond, so you use hardware
timers and interrupts (input capture), not slow polling. The resolution of your timer sets
the resolution of your speed.

Rejecting ambient light: Sunlight and room light add a DC offset and flicker. A focused
laser well above the ambient level, a threshold set between the two, and a shielded
detector keep the beam-break reliable indoors and out.

## build steps
## interview questions
Build one beam-detector

Aim a laser at a photodiode across a small gap, with a load resistor to make a voltage.
Read it on a scope or ADC and confirm the voltage drops hard when you block the beam.
Add a comparator

Feed the photodiode voltage to an LM393 with a threshold set between “beam” and
“blocked.” Confirm a clean HIGH / LOW edge as you break the beam, with no chatter.
Duplicate for two gates

Build a second identical beam-detector and mount both a known distance d apart along the
path, lasers aligned onto their detectors. Measure d precisely — it sets your accuracy.
Time the crossing

On the microcontroller, capture the timestamp of beam-A break and beam-B break with
hardware timing, compute Δt, and print it. Drop a ball through both beams to test.
Convert and display

Compute speed = d / Δt in m/s and mph, show it on serial or an OLED, and add an “armed”
state. Now clock darts, balls, or anything that crosses — your optical speed trap.

❯ project 02
Laser Rangefinder (Time-of-Flight LiDAR)
Measure distance with a pulse of light — the sensor inside every self-driving car

$25
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

Radar measures distance with radio; LiDAR does it with light. A time-of-flight sensor fires a
pulse of infrared light, measures how long it takes to bounce back, and multiplies by the
speed of light to get range — millimetre-accurate, dozens of times a second. Building one
around a module like the VL53L1X gets you a working laser rangefinder in an afternoon, and
understanding what it does underneath — pulse timing versus phase, the speed of light, photon
statistics — is the foundation of every autonomous-vehicle and robotics perception stack.
This is the headline build, and it feeds straight into the scanner in project 3.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand time-of-flight ranging, the difference between direct (pulsed) and
indirect (phase) ToF, why timing light is hard, signal-to-noise and averaging, and the
I2C sensor integration real perception systems are built on. LiDAR is one of the hottest
hiring areas in EE right now.

→ the job this maps to: autonomous vehicles, robotics, and LiDAR engineering — AV companies,
robotics firms, and LiDAR sensor makers (a direct companion to radar roles).

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t try to time light yourself — picosecond timing needs a dedicated chip. Start with
a VL53L1X (short range, indoor) or a TFmini (longer range); both hand you millimetres
over I2C, so you focus on using the data and, in project 3, scanning it.
## key design decisions

Time-of-flight, literally: The sensor emits a short IR pulse and measures the round-trip
time t to the target. Distance = c·t/2. Light travels ~30 cm per nanosecond, so the timing
must be picosecond-class — which is why it lives inside a dedicated chip, not your Arduino.

Direct vs indirect ToF: Direct ToF times a sharp pulse’s return (good at long range).
Indirect (AMCW) ToF modulates the beam and measures the phase shift of the returning light
to infer time — easier electronically, and what many compact modules and depth cameras use.

The SPAD detector: Modules like the VL53L1X use single-photon avalanche diodes that
register individual photons, plus on-chip timing, to resolve those tiny intervals and
reject ambient light by histogramming returns.

Range, accuracy, averaging: A single shot is noisy, so the sensor fires many pulses and
histograms them to pull the true range out of photon noise. More averaging means better
accuracy but a lower update rate — the classic ranging tradeoff.

Reading it over I2C: The module does the physics and hands you a distance in millimetres
over I2C. Your job is configuration (timing budget, region of interest, range mode) and
using the result — exactly the integration work real perception engineers do.

Why light instead of ultrasound for ranging? Light gives a tight beam (fine angular
resolution), works at long range, and is fast — you can scan it into a detailed map.
Ultrasound is cheaper but has a wide beam and low resolution. That tight beam is precisely
what makes the LiDAR mapping in project 3 possible.

Why does timing light need a dedicated chip? Light covers 30 cm per nanosecond, so
resolving centimetres means timing to tens of picoseconds — far beyond a microcontroller.
SPAD arrays and on-chip time-to-digital converters do this; you buy that capability in the
module rather than building it.

Why average so many pulses? Each returned pulse is buried in ambient light and shot noise.
By firing thousands of pulses and histogramming arrival times, the sensor finds the true
peak and rejects background — trading update rate for accuracy, which you tune with the
timing budget.

## interview questions
Wire the ToF module

Connect the module over I2C (SDA / SCL + power), load the vendor library, read a single
distance, and confirm it tracks your hand moving toward and away from the sensor.
Tune the timing budget

Set the range mode and timing budget (short / medium / long). Watch how a longer budget
improves accuracy and stability but slows the update rate — feel the accuracy-vs-speed
tradeoff directly.
Calibrate against a tape

Compare readings to a real tape measure at several distances. Note where it’s accurate,
where it drifts, and how target colour and reflectivity change the reading. Apply any
offset.
Live distance readout

Show the distance on an OLED with a fast refresh, plus min / max hold. Point it around
the room and watch it measure walls, objects, and the ceiling.
Stress-test the limits

Find its max range on a dark vs white target, test it outdoors (ambient IR hurts range),
and note the failure modes. You now understand a ToF sensor well enough to scan with it
next.

❯ project 03
Spinning LiDAR Room Scanner
Spin a rangefinder and watch your room appear as a point cloud

$45
intermediate
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

One distance reading is a number; thousands of them swept through a circle is a map. Mount
your time-of-flight sensor on a rotating platform, log distance against angle as it spins,
and plot the result — the outline of your room appears as a 2D point cloud, exactly like the
LiDAR on a robot vacuum or the spinning sensor on an early self-driving car. This is the most
visual build in the guide and the bridge from “I measured a distance” to “I perceived a
space,” which is the heart of robot navigation and SLAM.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand synchronising a sensor reading to an angular position, polar-to-Cartesian
conversion, point-cloud construction, and the data path from a raw sensor to a usable
map — foundational robotics-perception and SLAM groundwork.

→ the job this maps to: robotics, autonomous navigation, and perception engineering — robot-
vacuum and AMR makers, drone companies, and SLAM teams.
## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t machine a precision scanner. A stepper (or geared DC motor with an encoder) plus
your project-2 ToF module is enough; send data off the spinning platform over a slip
ring, or mount the electronics on the rotor and stream over BLE / Wi-Fi.

Distance plus angle: A LiDAR map is just many (angle, distance) pairs. Rotate the ToF
sensor and, at each angle, take a reading. The accuracy of your angle (from the motor) and
distance (from the sensor) sets the quality of the map.

Knowing the angle: A stepper gives you angle for free (count steps); a DC motor needs an
encoder or a once-per-revolution index mark to know where “zero” is. Synchronising each
distance sample to the correct angle is the core challenge.

Getting data off the spinner: Either run a slip ring for power and data, or — simpler — put
the microcontroller and sensor on the rotating platform and stream readings out over
Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, with only power crossing the slip ring (or a battery onboard).

Polar to Cartesian: Each (θ, r) becomes a point x = r·cosθ, y = r·sinθ. Plotting all the
points for one revolution draws the walls and objects around the sensor — your 2D point
cloud.

From scan to map: Stack revolutions and you can filter noise, detect walls, and (with
motion) start stitching scans together — the first step toward SLAM, where a robot builds a
map while tracking its own position.

## interview questions
Spin the sensor

Mount the ToF module on the stepper / motor platform and get it rotating smoothly at a
steady rate. Confirm the sensor still reads distance while spinning.
Tag readings with angle

Sync each distance sample to the motor angle (step count, or encoder + index pulse).
Verify that a known object in a known direction shows up at the right angle.
Stream the data out

Send (angle, distance) pairs to a laptop over BLE / Wi-Fi (or through a slip ring).
Confirm a continuous stream of pairs for each full revolution.
Plot the point cloud

On the laptop, convert each pair to x, y and plot one revolution. Your room’s outline
should appear. Tune speed and sample rate for a clean scan.
Refine and map

Average multiple revolutions to cut noise, mask the mount’s own structure, and watch the
map sharpen. Move the scanner and see how the cloud shifts — the doorway to SLAM.

❯ project 04
Laser Data Link (Free-Space Optical Comms)
Send audio and data across the room on a beam of light

$20
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

Fibre-optic internet is just light carrying data down a glass thread — and you can do the
same thing through open air with a laser and a photodiode. Modulate a laser’s brightness with
an audio or digital signal, point it at a photodiode across the room, and recover the signal
on the far side: a free-space optical link, the same idea as Li-Fi and satellite laser comms.
It is a hands-on lesson in modulation, analog front ends, and why light is such a high-
bandwidth carrier — and unlike radio it needs no licence and barely leaks past the beam.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand intensity modulation of an optical source, transimpedance photodiode
receivers, bandwidth and signal-to-noise in an analog link, and the basics of free-space
optics — which maps onto optical-comms, fibre, and photonics engineering.

→ the job this maps to: optical communications and photonics engineering — fibre and datacom
companies, free-space-optics and satellite-comms teams.
## how it works

Intensity modulation: The simplest optical link varies the laser’s brightness in step with
your signal. For audio, you add the audio to the laser’s drive current so the light
flickers with the waveform; a photodiode on the far end sees that flicker.

The transimpedance receiver: The photodiode produces a tiny current proportional to
received light. A transimpedance amplifier (op-amp + feedback resistor) converts it to a
usable voltage with enough bandwidth for your signal — the heart of every optical receiver.

Analog vs digital: Sending audio (analog AM on light) is the easy first version. Sending
digital data (on-off keying, UART over light) is the next step: now you care about bit
rate, thresholding, and clean edges rather than fidelity.

Bandwidth, and why light wins: The optical carrier is hundreds of terahertz, so the
available bandwidth dwarfs radio — which is why fibre and laser links carry so much data.
Your build’s actual speed is limited by the emitter and receiver electronics, not the
light.

Alignment and noise: A tight beam makes the link private and interference-resistant, but
you must aim it. Ambient light adds noise and offset, so you AC-couple the receiver (and
modulate above the flicker of room lights) to keep the signal clean.

Build the transmitter

Drive the laser / LED with a transistor so its brightness follows your signal. For

Build the receiver

Wire a photodiode into an op-amp transimpedance amplifier. Point a steady light at it

Close the link with audio

Aim the transmitter at the receiver across a gap, feed music into the transmitter, and
amplify the receiver output to a speaker. You should hear the audio carried on the beam.
Reject ambient light

AC-couple the receiver and shield it so room light doesn’t swamp the signal. Note how
alignment and distance change the received level.
Go digital (optional)

Switch to on-off keying and send UART bytes over the beam between two microcontrollers.
Measure the maximum reliable bit rate and see what limits it.

❯ project 05
Laser Vibrometer
Read a surface's vibration with a reflected beam — non-contact sensing with light

$30
advanced
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

Point a laser at a reflective surface, catch the reflected dot on a photodiode, and any
vibration of that surface changes the light reaching your detector — letting you read the
surface’s motion without touching it. This is laser vibrometry, a real engineering technique
for measuring how speakers, motors, and structures vibrate without loading them down.
Building one teaches optical detection of tiny displacements, signal recovery from a noisy
photodetector, and the limits of non-contact sensing. It is one of the most striking
demonstrations of how much information a single beam of light carries.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand optical displacement and vibration sensing, recovering a small AC signal
from a photodetector, filtering and amplification, and the practical limits of non-
contact measurement — which maps onto optical metrology, acoustics, and structural-
health-monitoring work.

→ the job this maps to: optical metrology and sensing engineering — acoustics labs,
structural-health monitoring, and precision-measurement teams.

! MEASURE YOUR OWN SURFACES ONLY
This is a vibration-sensing technique for surfaces and devices you own — a speaker cone,
a motor housing, a panel on your own bench. Do not point it at other people’s windows,
rooms, or property to capture sound or conversations: that is eavesdropping, it is
illegal in most places, and it is not what this build is for. Keep it on your own
equipment.

Light carries surface motion: When a laser reflects off a surface, the reflected beam’s
direction and the light coupled back into your detector depend on the surface’s exact
position. Vibrate the surface and the photodiode sees a matching AC signal riding on the
reflection.

The detector geometry: A simple setup catches the reflected dot at the edge of a photodiode
(or through a slit) so small angular shifts change how much light lands on the sensor —
converting tiny surface motions into a measurable voltage swing.

Recovering a tiny signal: The vibration signal is small and sits on a large DC level from
the steady reflection. AC-coupling, a low-noise amplifier, and band-pass filtering pull the
vibration (an audio-band signal from a speaker, say) out of the background.

Why it is hard: The signal depends heavily on surface reflectivity, alignment, and ambient
light, and it is easily swamped by noise or a poor reflector. Stable mounting and a
cooperative, shiny target are what make it work.

What the pros do: True laser Doppler vibrometers interfere the reflected beam with a
reference to read sub-wavelength motion precisely. Your build is the intuition-level
version of that instrument — same idea, far simpler optics.

Set up a stable reflection

Mount the laser and a target surface (e.g. a small mirror taped to a speaker you own)

Build the receiver

Convert the photodiode current to voltage, AC-couple it, and add a low-noise band-pass

On your own equipment, test how reflectivity, distance, and alignment change the result,

❯ project 06
Structured-Light 3D Scanner
Sweep a laser line across an object and rebuild it in 3D

$40
advanced
2 weekends
## why this matters

A camera sees a flat image; add a laser and geometry and you can recover depth. Project a
thin laser line onto an object, watch from a camera offset to one side, and the line bends
along the object’s contours — measure that bend and triangulation gives you the surface’s 3D
shape. Sweep the line across the object and you reconstruct a full 3D model, the same
structured-light principle behind many 3D scanners and depth cameras. It is the most
ambitious optical build here and a direct lesson in the camera-plus-light geometry at the
core of 3D vision.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand triangulation, camera-laser calibration, extracting a laser line from an
image, and reconstructing 3D points from 2D observations — core 3D-vision, metrology,
and depth-sensing engineering.

→ the job this maps to: 3D vision, metrology, and depth-sensing engineering — 3D-scanning and
CV companies, robotics perception, and industrial-inspection teams.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t build custom optics. A line-laser module (a dot laser with a cylindrical lens), a
webcam offset to one side, and a turntable or slow manual sweep are enough; the geometry
and the image processing are where the real work — and learning — live.

Triangulation, not timing: Unlike ToF, structured light gets depth from geometry. The
laser, the camera, and a point on the object form a triangle; knowing the laser-to-camera
baseline and angles, you solve for the point’s distance — the same principle as your two
eyes judging depth.

The bending line: A flat reference plane shows the laser line straight. An object pushes
parts of the line sideways in the camera image; how far each pixel of the line shifts
encodes how far that part of the surface is from the reference — a depth profile in one
shot.

Finding the line in the image: For each camera row you find the brightest (reddest) pixel —
the laser line’s position, to sub-pixel accuracy. Robust line extraction under ambient
light is the key image-processing step.

Calibration: You must know the geometry: the angle of the laser plane and the camera’s
parameters and position. A calibration step using known reference distances turns pixel
shifts into real millimetres.

Sweeping to a model: One line gives one slice. Rotate the object on a turntable (or sweep
the line) while capturing slices, then stack them into a full 3D point cloud or mesh you
can view and export.

## build steps
## interview questions
Build the rig

Fix a line laser and a webcam a known distance apart (a baseline), with the camera
viewing the laser line on a reference plane. Rigidity is essential — any flex corrupts
the geometry.
Extract the laser line

In OpenCV, isolate the laser line (colour threshold) and find its position per image row
to sub-pixel accuracy. Confirm a clean line trace even with some room light.
Calibrate the geometry

Using known distances on the reference plane, work out how a pixel shift of the line
maps to a real depth. Validate against an object of known size.
Capture one profile

Place an object so the line drapes over it; the bent line is one depth slice. Convert
the bend to 3D points and plot that single profile.
Sweep and reconstruct

Rotate the object on a turntable (or sweep the line) capturing many slices, stack them
into a point cloud, and view / export your 3D model. Refine lighting and calibration for
a clean scan.

❯ wrap

Light is the fastest instrument you own —
point it and read what comes back.

A break-beam, a time-of-flight pulse, a spinning rangefinder, a modulated beam, a reflected
dot, a bent laser line — six ways to turn light into information: distance, shape, motion,
and data. The optics are cheap (a $3 laser, a $2 photodiode, a webcam), and just like radar,
the real skill is in the front end and the signal processing: the detection, the timing, the
triangulation, the filtering. That is exactly what optical-sensing, LiDAR, and photonics
teams hire for.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
photodetection →time-of-flight →LiDAR scanning →optical comms →vibrometry →structured
light

! LASER SAFETY, EVERY TIME
Use only low-power Class 1 / 2 modules, never look into a beam or aim one at anyone, and
respect that infrared lasers are invisible. And keep the vibrometer pointed only at
surfaces you own — not anyone else’s windows.

DO THIS
Build even one of these. Capture the output — a speed readout, a point cloud of your
room, audio carried on a beam, a 3D scan — and put it on GitHub with a clear README, the
geometry or calibration you used, and an honest note on scope. One optics demo and one
clean repo prove you can pull real information out of light.

Full build notes, parts links, and the next field guide go out in The Build List. The
people actually shipping these — and trading alignment and calibration tricks — are in
Ohm’s Club.
